newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Selling pressure hits Irish pound on EMU concerns.
newsitem.headline: Selling pressure hits Irish pound on EMU concerns.

text.p: The Irish pound plummeted on Wednesday, succumbing to strong selling pressures which had been building in anticipation of Ireland's perceived desire to enter European Monetary Union (EMU) at the median rate of 2.41 marks.

Economists said rumours that Ireland's central bank, which had been intervening heavily to shore up the Irish unit in recent weeks, had decided to let the currency fall filtered through the market late on Tuesday.

"Last night it emerged that the central bank was going to let the punt drift down," one currency trader said. "There was already a lot of speculators out there putting strong selling pressure on the punt and the Bank obviously decided to step back for awhile."
The rumour opened the floodgates for large volume, mainly foreign, selling of the punt, the trader said.

The Irish unit sharply underperformed on otherwise subdued crosses in early trade, hitting the weakest level against the mark in more than a month and slumping to the lowest against sterling since August 1993.

"If Ireland joins EMU, which the market now considers a sure thing, then it will have to be at a mid-rate of 2.40 to 2.41 against the mark. This morning it has dropped to below 2.60 marks but it still has a long way to go," one trader said.
The Irish pound continued to slide throughout the morning and was trading at 0.9120/60 stg and 2.5700/00 marks by 1056 GMT versus late Tuesday's European levels of 0.9485 and 2.6705.
Traders said the market expected the central bank, which has continued to act to smooth fluctuations in the currency over recent months, to intervene to set a new floor under the punt before long.

"As we approach EMU the market perception is that the Irish pound has to weaken because from the 1/1/1999 levels will be set in perpetuity. Going in over 2.60 against the mark would pose significant long term competitive difficulties," Bank of Ireland Group Treasury economist Colin Hunt said.
Traders said the central bank can only smooth out the punt's decline.
"The market believes that it would be unrealistic for the Irish currency to join EMU at its current level. It has to fall and a rate of 90 pence sterling is not impossible," one dealer added.

Dealers said the Irish pound remained near the top of the ERM grid 7.37 percent above the weakest currency, the French franc by 1056 GMT on Wednesday, compared with 11.37 percent above the same unit on Tuesday.
Money market rates rose briskly in response to the punt's weakness. One-month rates were quoted at 6.00/6.25 percent, against 5.81/5.94 at Tuesday's close.
The official Short Term Facility rate (STF), which is considered a ceiling rate, is set at 6.25 percent.

"The interbank rates are up dramatically reflecting the selling pressure on the punt," Riada economist Padraic Garvey said. Garvey said that if current interbank rates are sustained or move higher it is likely to lead to upward press on retail rates.
